talks.title: Wrap Up
talks.teaser: Discusses wrap Up and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: A brief No Hat conference wrap-up featuring attendee testimonials about community, international participation, and the conference's growth across four parallel tracks.

Key Topics: No Hat as an established European security conference; international speaker and attendee participation; Research, Technical, Workshop, and Executive tracks; and attendee perspectives on community and camaraderie.

Technical Details: Short interview clips from attendees including Katie Moussouris (Luta Security), Mario Polino, and others discussing their presentations on virtualization, AI in bug bounty, password managers, and threat actor attribution.

Takeaways: No Hat continues growing as a European security community hub with diverse tracks serving researchers, practitioners, and executives.

talks.title: Federico Maggi - [Keynote] Secure AI Starts with Solid Compute Foundations
talks.teaser: Details federico Maggi - [Keynote] Secure AI Starts with Solid Compute Foundations and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
AI Stack Under the Hood

Trend Micro/Federico Maggi’s No Hat keynote traces modern AI from HTTP-authenticated microservices down through containers, VMs, and servers to LLM frameworks that iteratively predict next tokens trained on text, code, and security-relevant content. Agentic systems add orchestration across LLMs, APIs, and MCP-style tools.

Compute Foundations for LLMs

Transformers embed tokens, apply layered numerical transformations, and output probability distributions over vocabulary. Training trillions of parameters demands specialized scale beyond general-purpose CPUs—GPUs parallelize locally; ASICs like AWS Trainium 2 use systolic arrays fed directly from high-bandwidth memory without traditional instruction streams.

Accelerator Security Boundary

Trainium cards include a management SOC controlling reset, PCIe setup, and security configuration. Maggi’s threat model assumes cloud tenants may run as root with custom drivers, so the management microcontroller must enforce isolation at the machine level—secure AI, he argues, starts with trustworthy compute hardware beneath models and agents.

talks.title: Efstratios Chatzoglou - Unmasking Credential Leaks: A Security Evaluation of ...
talks.teaser: Demonstrates efstratios Chatzoglou - Unmasking Credential Leaks: A Security Evaluation of and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Research Questions and Threat Model

University of Piraeus researchers asked which password managers, browser built-ins, and VPN clients store plaintext credentials in process memory, and how often those secrets repeat. Testing assumes standard user access, an unlocked vault, and ability to run OS commands—typical post-compromise conditions—not admin rights.

Scope and Methodology

The two-year study (July 2023–March 2025) examined 12 desktop password managers, five browsers, 12 browser extensions, and 21 commercial and enterprise VPNs. Primary scenarios dump process memory while apps are open; VPN tests also cover cases where credentials persist without re-prompting.

Findings Across Product Classes

Most tested password managers leaked master passwords and vault entries, often many times per dump. All evaluated Mac browsers exposed credentials in memory; extensions varied. Commercial VPNs showed fewer leaks than enterprise VPNs, where domain credentials in memory pose lateral-movement risk.

Pandora Tool and Vendor Response

The team released Pandora, an open-source extractor using pattern-based memory scanning, and assigned CVEs to vendors including Kaspersky, Passbolt, and Fortinet. Chatzoglou discusses how staggered disclosure timelines revealed uneven vendor remediation and why memory hygiene remains an underappreciated attack path.

talks.title: E. Pennucci, A. Repola - Go with the (net)flow: a tale of fixing ML-based network ...
talks.teaser: Examines E. Pennucci, A. Repola - Go with the (net)flow: a tale of fixing ML-based network and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
ML for network intrusion detection

Hermes Pennucci and Antonio Repola from Inexa Defense review machine-learning-based network intrusion detection, covering popular tools, bugs they found, and their open-source NetFlowMeter feature extractor. Neural approaches excel at pattern recognition but depend on reliable flow statistics.

Why CICFlowMeter failed at scale

While automating large PCAP pipelines, sub-gigabyte files triggered JVM out-of-memory errors even on upgraded hardware. Source review showed an unmaintainable C/Java mix with poor documentation, prompting a full rewrite rather than incremental patching.

NetFlowMeter improvements

Their replacement addresses TCP reset-flag handling bugs where a flow starting with RST was allocated but never terminated, causing resource leaks when combined with flow cutting. They also experiment with removing idle-timeout features that most public datasets assume at default values, showing early promise for cleaner ML training data.
